kawasaki-disease.name: Kawasaki disease
kawasaki-disease.scope: Diagnostic criteria (CRASH and burn), echocardiography, coronary artery aneurysms, intravenous immunoglobulin, aspirin, refractory disease
kawasaki-disease.core: Persistent fever with mucocutaneous inflammation in a young child suggests Kawasaki disease; early treatment reduces coronary artery injury.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Usually age <5 years; more common in children of East Asian ancestry
Infants, delayed diagnosis, and early coronary abnormalities increase complication risk

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Fever ≥5 days + ≥4 CRASH features**; experienced clinicians may diagnose earlier when classic
C: bilateral nonpurulent conjunctivitis; R: polymorphous rash; A: cervical adenopathy, usually unilateral >1.5 cm
S: oral strawberry tongue/cracked red lips; H: hand/foot erythema/edema → later periungual peeling
Irritability, sterile pyuria, ↑ESR/CRP; thrombocytosis typically after first week, not required initially

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immune-mediated medium-vessel vasculitis preferentially injures coronary arteries
Inflammation weakens arterial walls → dilation/aneurysm, thrombosis, and later stenosis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis + echocardiography** at presentation; normal initial echo does not exclude disease
Prolonged unexplained fever with 2–3 features, especially infant → incomplete-disease inflammatory/echo algorithm
CBC, CRP/ESR, albumin, liver tests, urinalysis support assessment; no single confirmatory laboratory test
Repeat echo at approximately 1–2 and 4–6 weeks; more frequent for coronary abnormalities

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **IVIG + aspirin promptly**, ideally within first 10 days; treat later if ongoing inflammation/coronary disease
Acute anti-inflammatory aspirin → low-dose antiplatelet phase after afebrile; duration follows coronary findings
★ High-risk disease → consider **adjunct glucocorticoids** with initial IVIG through specialist team
Fever ≥36 hours after IVIG → reassess; repeat IVIG, infliximab, or steroids for refractory disease
Large/giant aneurysms → additional anticoagulation with cardiology; manage shock/myocarditis supportively

rows.label: Complications
items: Coronary aneurysm, thrombosis, MI → ischemic heart failure; myocarditis, ventricular dysfunction, valvular regurgitation
IVIG can cause hemolysis; aspirin increases bleeding and Reye risk during influenza/varicella

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ After IVIG, **delay MMR/varicella approximately 11 months**; maintain cardiology follow-up
Annual inactivated influenza vaccination while receiving aspirin; promptly discuss varicella exposure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Adenovirus: exudative conjunctivitis/pharyngitis; scarlet fever: positive streptococcal testing, no coronary involvement
MIS-C: recent SARS-CoV-2, older child, marked GI symptoms/shock, often thrombocytopenia
DRESS: recent drug, weeks' latency, facial edema, eosinophilia, hepatitis; conjunctivitis/strawberry tongue favor Kawasaki

neonatal-resuscitation.name: Neonatal resuscitation
neonatal-resuscitation.scope: NRP algorithm, initial steps (warm, dry, stimulate), PPV indications (apnea, HR < 100), chest compressions (HR < 60), epinephrine, target SpO2
neonatal-resuscitation.core: At birth, effective ventilation drives heart-rate recovery; escalate support according to the response after each timed intervention.

rows.label: Definition
items: Apgar: appearance, pulse, grimace, activity, respiration, each scored 0–2 at 1 and 5 min
Score 1: acrocyanosis, pulse <100, grimace, some flexion, irregular breathing

rows.label: Interpret
items: ★ **Right-hand preductal pulse oximetry**; targets: 2 min 65–70%, 5 min 80–85%, 10 min 85–95%
Auscultate HR initially; ECG improves continuous measurement during advanced support
Oxygen start: ≥35 wk **21%**; 32–34 wk 21–30%; <32 wk 30–100%, titrated

rows.label: Use when
items: Vigorous term newborn → skin-to-skin, routine care; defer cord clamping ≥60 seconds
★ Poor tone/breathing → **warm, dry, position airway, stimulate**; initial assessment within first minute
Spontaneous breathing plus distress/cyanosis → oxygen titration; consider CPAP

rows.label: Compare
items: ★ Poor PPV → **reposition, reseal, open mouth, suction obstruction, raise pressure, alternate airway**
Compressions: two-thumb encircling technique, depth one-third chest; 90 compressions + 30 breaths/min
Epinephrine: **0.01–0.03 mg/kg IV/IO**; repeat every 3–5 min; umbilical venous access preferred

rows.label: Traps
items: No routine suction, including meconium; suction only suspected airway obstruction
★ **2025 PPV rate 30–60/min**; older teaching 40–60/min
Persistent bradycardia → check pneumothorax/hypovolemia; blood loss → saline or uncrossmatched blood

table.title: Timed escalation
rows: Stop compressions; continue ventilation if needed

neurocutaneous-disorders.name: Neurocutaneous disorders
neurocutaneous-disorders.scope: Neurofibromatosis type 1, neurofibromatosis type 2, tuberous sclerosis, Sturge-Weber syndrome, von Hippel-Lindau disease, ataxia-telangiectasia
neurocutaneous-disorders.core: Characteristic skin or ocular lesions plus neurologic tumors, seizures, or progressive ataxia suggest an inherited or mosaic multisystem disorder.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: NF1, NF2-related schwannomatosis, TSC, VHL: autosomal dominant; frequent de novo variants
Ataxia-telangiectasia: autosomal recessive; Sturge-Weber: sporadic somatic mosaicism

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Changing painful neurofibroma**, rapid growth, or new weakness → malignant transformation concern
Early focal seizures or developmental regression → evaluate structural cerebral lesions
NF2: hearing loss/tinnitus; NF1: cutaneous neurofibromas and childhood learning difficulties

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Tumor suppressor dysfunction → hamartomas or neoplasms; ATM defect → impaired DNA repair

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical pattern + genetic testing**; targeted MRI for neurologic or tumor symptoms
NF1: ≥2 criteria; ≥6 café-au-lait macules, size >5 mm prepubertal, >15 mm postpubertal
TSC: two major features or one major plus two minor; pathogenic variant also diagnostic

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic tumors → specialist resection; TSC growing lesions → **everolimus** in selected cases
TSC infantile spasms → vigabatrin; other seizures → antiseizure drugs
Sturge-Weber seizures → levetiracetam; refractory focal epilepsy → surgical evaluation
Ataxia-telangiectasia: rehabilitation, infection treatment; minimize ionizing radiation

rows.label: Complications
items: NF1: malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor; VHL: renal carcinoma and pheochromocytoma
TSC: hydrocephalus, renal hemorrhage; ataxia-telangiectasia: lymphoma/leukemia, recurrent sinopulmonary infections

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Genetic counseling**; syndrome-specific eye, hearing, renal, and tumor surveillance
Sturge-Weber: ophthalmology follow-up for glaucoma; NF1: childhood BP and vision monitoring

rows.label: Mimics
items: Isolated café-au-lait macules: no additional diagnostic criteria
Friedreich ataxia: areflexia, cardiomyopathy, no ocular telangiectasias

table.title: Signature findings
rows: Axillary freckling, Lisch nodules, optic glioma
Ash-leaf macules, angiofibromas, cortical tubers, renal angiomyolipomas

neutropenia.name: Neutropenia
neutropenia.scope: Benign ethnic neutropenia (Duffy-null), drug-induced neutropenia, febrile neutropenia, autoimmune neutropenia, ANC thresholds, evaluation and management
neutropenia.core: Infection risk tracks the depth and duration of neutrophil depletion; fever with severe neutropenia is an antibiotic emergency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Cytotoxic chemotherapy, marrow malignancy, viral infection, autoimmune disease, B12/folate/copper deficiency
Clozapine, methimazole, propylthiouracil, TMP–SMX and other drugs can cause agranulocytosis
Duffy-null associated neutrophil counts: stable isolated reduction without increased infection risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Oral ulcers, gingivitis, recurrent bacterial/fungal infections; inflammatory signs and pus may be absent
Cyclic mouth ulcers/infections suggest cyclic neutropenia; multiple cytopenias suggest marrow disease
Drug-associated fever or sore throat → urgent CBC, especially with antithyroid drugs

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced marrow production, peripheral destruction or splenic sequestration lowers circulating neutrophils
Mucosal barrier injury plus impaired innate defense permits rapid invasive bacterial infection

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ANC = WBC × (% neutrophils + bands)/100**; repeat CBC with differential and smear
Mild: 1000–1500/µL; moderate: 500–1000; **severe <500**; profound <100
★ Febrile neutropenia: **≥38.3°C once or ≥38.0°C for ≥1 hour**, ANC <500 or expected decline
Obtain peripheral/line blood cultures, targeted cultures and imaging without delaying antibiotics
Persistent unexplained severe counts, abnormal smear or other cytopenias → marrow evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Febrile severe neutropenia → **IV cefepime**, piperacillin–tazobactam or meropenem promptly
Add vancomycin for shock, suspected line/skin infection, pneumonia or documented resistant gram-positive infection
★ Stop culprit drug; G-CSF for selected severe/drug-related cases and high-risk chemotherapy settings
Carefully selected low-risk stable patients → oral ciprofloxacin + amoxicillin–clavulanate with reliable close follow-up
High-risk persistent fever 4–7 days → fungal evaluation and empiric **caspofungin**

rows.label: Complications
items: Pseudomonas sepsis, invasive candidiasis/aspergillosis, neutropenic enterocolitis; avoid rectal instrumentation
**Ecthyma gangrenosum**: bulla → painless black necrotic ulcer, Pseudomonas bacteremia; antipseudomonal drug, not steroids

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hand hygiene, oral care; selected prolonged profound neutropenia → antibacterial/antifungal prophylaxis
Stable Duffy-null pattern → reassurance after excluding other causes; no unnecessary G-CSF

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lymphopenia: opportunistic infection risk with preserved ANC
Acute leukemia: blasts and additional cytopenias

newborn-screening.name: Newborn screening
newborn-screening.scope: Congenital hypothyroidism (macroglossia, umbilical hernia, levothyroxine), phenylketonuria, galactosemia, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, hemoglobinopathies, cystic fibrosis, pulse oximetry, hearing screen
newborn-screening.core: Screen apparently healthy newborns for treatable metabolic, endocrine, genetic, cardiac, and hearing disorders before symptoms or irreversible injury.

rows.label: Who
items: All newborns; blood-spot panels vary by state; also screen cardiac oxygenation and hearing

rows.label: Start/stop
items: ★ Heel stick **24–48 hours**; early collection, transfusion, prematurity may require repeats
Pulse oximetry ≥24 hours or before early discharge; hearing by 1 month

rows.label: Test
items: ★ Cardiac pass: **≥95% in both right hand and foot**, difference ≤3 percentage points
<90% anywhere → immediate failure; otherwise **one repeat** in 1 hour (older algorithms: two)
Hearing: otoacoustic emissions or auditory brainstem response; NICU → brainstem-based screen

rows.label: IF positive
items: ★ Critical result → confirm promptly without delaying lifesaving treatment
Failed cardiac screen → evaluate hypoxemia, echocardiography; ductal-dependent lesion → prostaglandin E1
★ Failed hearing → diagnostic audiology by **3 months**, intervention by **6 months**

rows.label: Traps
items: Normal examination does not exclude disease; hypothyroidism later causes macroglossia/umbilical hernia
Ill infant with suspected CAH → treat despite pending screen; no diagnostic reassurance
Hereditary fructose intolerance: symptoms only after fructose/sucrose, so not on breast milk alone

table.title: Urgent positive blood-spot results
rows: Start levothyroxine promptly, ideally by 2 weeks
Classic galactosemia: feeding → vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly
Penicillin from infancy, vaccines, hematology follow-up
Specialty care, nutrition, pancreatic enzymes if insufficient

normal-pediatric-variants.name: Normal pediatric variants
normal-pediatric-variants.scope: Thymic sail sign on chest radiograph, physiologic genu varum and valgum, tibial torsion, infantile hemangioma
normal-pediatric-variants.core: Age-appropriate anatomy and growth can resemble disease; symmetry, normal function, and expected evolution support reassurance instead of unnecessary intervention.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Normal skeletal alignment changes with development; familial rotational profiles are common
Infantile hemangiomas more frequent with prematurity, low birth weight and female sex

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Symmetric painless findings with normal growth/function** favor physiologic variation
Asymmetry, pain, progression, short stature or abnormal neurologic examination → pathologic evaluation
Hemangiomas appear in first weeks, proliferate rapidly during infancy, then gradually involute
Periocular, airway/beard-distribution, ulcerating or large segmental lesions are high-risk, not simple cosmetic variants

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Growth remodels lower-limb alignment/rotation; normal thymic tissue may silhouette against the lung
Hemangioma is a benign vascular tumor with proliferative and involution phases, distinct from vascular malformation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical symmetric limb variant → **clinical examination**, growth review and rotational profile
Imaging for red flags, atypical age or suspected metabolic bone disease; not routine physiologic bowing
Typical hemangioma → clinical diagnosis; ≥5 cutaneous lesions → hepatic ultrasound
Large segmental facial/lumbosacral lesion → evaluate associated structural anomalies with specialist guidance

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Reassurance and observation** for physiologic alignment, thymic appearance, toddler genital self-touching without abuse signs
Special shoes/braces do not correct internal tibial torsion; persistent severe functional deformity → orthopedics
★ High-risk hemangioma → **early referral, oral propranolol**; selected superficial lesions → topical timolol
Give propranolol with feeds, hold during poor intake/vomiting; monitor bradycardia and hypoglycemia

rows.label: Complications
items: Unnecessary imaging, bracing or surgery; hemangioma → ulceration, amblyopia, airway obstruction or residual skin change
Multiple hepatic hemangiomas → high-output heart failure or consumptive hypothyroidism

rows.label: Mimics
items: Blount disease: progressive asymmetric tibial bowing; rickets: widened wrists, abnormal mineralization
Mediastinal mass: mass effect/distortion rather than soft thymic contour

osteomyelitis.name: Osteomyelitis
osteomyelitis.scope: Vertebral osteomyelitis and discitis, hematogenous seeding (S. aureus, IV drug use), contiguous spread (diabetic foot ulcer), probe-to-bone test, MRI, bone biopsy and culture, parenteral antibiotics
osteomyelitis.core: Persistent focal bone or back pain, especially with bacteremia, a deep diabetic ulcer, or elevated inflammatory markers, suggests bone infection.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hematogenous seeding: S. aureus, endocarditis, injection drug use; vertebral disease often lacks fever
Contiguous spread: diabetic foot ulcers, pressure injury; direct inoculation: open fracture, surgery, hardware
Sickle cell: Salmonella association, but S. aureus remains important; plantar puncture through shoe → Pseudomonas

rows.label: Clues
items: Point tenderness, swelling, drainage or nonhealing sinus; systemic toxicity may be absent
★ New neurologic deficit, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention → **epidural extension/cord compression**
Diabetic ulcer over bony prominence, visible bone, or prolonged failure to heal increases suspicion
Child: fever, point tenderness over long-bone **metaphysis**; septic joint instead limits joint motion

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Infected bone develops inflammatory pressure, vascular compromise, and necrosis
Sequestrum: devitalized infected bone; involucrum: reactive new bone; biofilm promotes hardware persistence

rows.label: Dx
items: CBC, ESR/CRP, two blood-culture sets; plain films first but early findings can be absent
★ Diabetic foot: **probe-to-bone** plus radiographs/inflammatory markers; MRI if diagnosis remains uncertain
★ **MRI** best for early marrow disease and epidural/paraspinal abscess; bone scan uptake if MRI unavailable
Bone biopsy for histology/culture before antibiotics if stable; superficial wound swabs unreliable
Compatible vertebral MRI plus S. aureus bacteremia usually obviates biopsy; assess endocarditis source

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Sepsis or neurologic compromise → cultures then **IV vancomycin + cefepime**, urgent surgical assessment
Stable vertebral disease → obtain microbiologic diagnosis before empiric antibiotics
MSSA → cefazolin/nafcillin; MRSA → vancomycin; tailor to cultures, usually about **6 weeks**
IV initially for serious disease; selected stable patients can complete highly bioavailable oral regimens
Debride necrotic bone/drain abscess; surgery for instability, progressive deficit, or uncontrolled infection

rows.label: Complications
items: Epidural abscess, pathologic fracture, deformity, bacteremia, chronic draining sinus
Longstanding sinus may develop squamous carcinoma; prolonged antibiotics → line infection, renal injury, C. difficile

rows.label: Prevention
items: Diabetic foot inspection, offloading, vascular assessment, glucose control; prompt open-fracture antibiotics and debridement

rows.label: Mimics
items: Charcot arthropathy: neuropathic warm foot, joint fragmentation; MRI/biopsy may distinguish overlapping infection
Bone malignancy: destructive mass, pathology without infection
Degenerative disc disease: mechanical pain without infectious endplate/disc pattern

pediatric-abdominal-masses.name: Pediatric abdominal masses
pediatric-abdominal-masses.scope: Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma, WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann), neuroblastoma (adrenal medulla, crosses midline, catecholamines, N-myc), hydronephrosis, hepatoblastoma, ultrasound evaluation
pediatric-abdominal-masses.core: A child's abdominal mass: establish its organ of origin before biopsy; renal, sympathetic, hepatic, and obstructive lesions require different management.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ Wilms: **WAGR**—aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, intellectual disability
Wilms: Beckwith-Wiedemann—macroglossia, omphalocele, hemihyperplasia
Hepatoblastoma: very low birth weight, Beckwith-Wiedemann, familial adenomatous polyposis
Hydronephrosis: congenital urinary obstruction or vesicoureteral reflux

rows.label: Clues
items: Often found incidentally during bathing; persistent enlargement, weight loss, pallor suggest malignancy
Neuroblastoma dissemination: periorbital ecchymoses, bone pain; opsoclonus-myoclonus possible
★ Weakness, gait change, bladder dysfunction → possible spinal cord compression

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Wilms: embryonal renal tumor; neuroblastoma: neural crest-derived adrenal medulla or sympathetic chain
Hepatoblastoma: embryonal hepatic malignancy; hydronephrosis: collecting-system dilation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Abdominal ultrasound** first → solid versus cystic and renal versus extrarenal origin
Solid lesion → contrast CT/MRI abdomen; chest imaging for malignant staging
Neuroblastoma: tissue diagnosis, MYCN testing, MIBG imaging, bone marrow assessment for staging
MYCN amplification → unfavorable prognosis; age and stage also determine neuroblastoma risk

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected Wilms: avoid repeated vigorous palpation and routine percutaneous biopsy; US approach usually nephrectomy first
Wilms: surgery + vincristine/dactinomycin-based chemotherapy; radiation for higher-risk disease
Neuroblastoma: low risk → observation/resection; high risk → chemotherapy, surgery, transplant, anti-GD2 immunotherapy
Hepatoblastoma: cisplatin-based chemotherapy + resection; unresectable liver-confined disease → transplant evaluation
Hydronephrosis: infected obstruction → urgent drainage; progressive functional loss → corrective surgery

rows.label: Complications
items: Tumor rupture/spillage worsens Wilms staging; bilateral disease threatens renal function
Hydronephrosis → infection, renal injury; neuroblastoma → marrow failure or cord compression

rows.label: Prevention
items: Syndrome-specific abdominal ultrasound surveillance for children predisposed to embryonal tumors

rows.label: Mimics
items: Constipation: fecal loading, improves after stool evacuation
Ovarian mass: pelvic/adnexal origin; torsion causes acute pain

pediatric-hip-disorders.name: Pediatric hip disorders
pediatric-hip-disorders.scope: Developmental dysplasia of the hip, Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, transient synovitis, pediatric limp workup
pediatric-hip-disorders.core: A child’s limp or knee pain may originate in the hip; age, weight-bearing ability, and hip rotation separate common developmental disorders.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Breech presentation, female sex, family history → developmental hip dysplasia
Obesity and adolescence → slipped capital femoral epiphysis; atypically young/thin cases suggest endocrine disease
Recent viral illness → transient synovitis; Perthes often boys aged 4–8 years

rows.label: Clues
items: Infant asymmetric abduction or leg length; older child limp, groin/thigh/knee pain
★ **Fever, toxic appearance, refusal to bear weight**, painful restricted motion → septic arthritis concern
SCFE: obligate external rotation with flexion, limited internal rotation/abduction; Perthes: gradual painless/painful limp with limited internal rotation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dysplasia: shallow acetabulum and unstable femoral head; Perthes: femoral-head avascular necrosis
SCFE: physeal failure displaces epiphysis relative to neck; synovitis: transient sterile joint inflammation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Examine hip in unexplained knee pain**: gait, rotation, fever; limited rotation → **hip x-ray**, not knee MRI
DDH: Ortolani reduces dislocation; Barlow provokes instability; limited abduction more useful after early infancy
Risk-based DDH imaging → ultrasound around 6 weeks; radiograph after femoral ossification, usually ≥4–6 months
Suspected septic hip → CBC, ESR/CRP, cultures, ultrasound for effusion → urgent aspiration
Kocher features: fever >38.5°C, nonweight-bearing, WBC >12,000, ESR >40; support concern, never replace aspiration

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected SCFE → **immediate nonweight-bearing**, orthopedic fixation; no forceful manipulation
★ Septic joint → **urgent drainage + IV antibiotics** after cultures when feasible
Transient synovitis → rest, NSAID, close reassessment; persistent/worsening symptoms require renewed evaluation
Perthes → orthopedic containment/ROM plan; DDH treatment depends on age and stability below

rows.label: Complications
items: Untreated dysplasia → early osteoarthritis; SCFE → avascular necrosis/chondrolysis
Perthes → femoral-head deformity; missed septic arthritis → irreversible joint destruction

rows.label: Prevention
items: Newborn and infant hip examinations; avoid tight swaddling with extended adducted hips

rows.label: Mimics
items: Osteomyelitis: focal bony tenderness, MRI marrow changes
Trauma: injury history and fracture imaging

table.title: Imaging and definitive branch
rows: Sclerosis, flattening, fragmentation; decreased bone-scan uptake

pediatric-hip-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric orthopedic assessment principles.

pediatric-neck-masses.name: Pediatric neck masses
pediatric-neck-masses.scope: Thyroglossal duct cyst, branchial cleft cyst, cystic hygroma (lymphatic malformation), congenital muscular torticollis (fibromatosis colli), cervical lymphadenitis
pediatric-neck-masses.core: Childhood neck lump: location, mobility with swallowing, tenderness, and head posture separate congenital remnants from inflammatory lymph nodes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Congenital anomalies may enlarge during URI; lymphatic malformation associated with Turner syndrome
Bacterial lymphadenitis: Staphylococcus aureus, group A Streptococcus; dental disease → oral anaerobes
Fibromatosis colli: infancy, intrauterine positioning or birth-related sternocleidomastoid injury

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Stridor, drooling, respiratory distress** → threatened airway; immediate stabilization
★ Hard, fixed, supraclavicular, enlarging mass or weight loss/night sweats → **malignancy evaluation**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Embryologic tract persistence, abnormal lymphatic channels, muscle fibrosis, or reactive/infected lymphoid tissue

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Neck ultrasound first** for superficial mass; distinguish cystic/solid lesions and detect abscess
Before midline cyst excision → confirm normally located thyroid; ectopic thyroid may be sole functioning tissue
Deep infection/airway compression → contrast CT; extensive lymphatic lesion → MRI
Persistent unexplained concerning node → excisional biopsy; CBC/differential guides hematologic evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Treat infection before elective congenital cyst surgery**
Toxic child, oral intolerance, or treatment failure → IV cefazolin; MRSA concern → vancomycin
Fluctuant bacterial abscess → drainage plus culture; dental source → amoxicillin-clavulanate

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent infection, abscess, airway compression; untreated torticollis → plagiocephaly and facial asymmetry

rows.label: Prevention
items: Complete tract removal reduces cyst recurrence; early positioning exercises prevent secondary deformity
Oral hygiene and dental treatment reduce odontogenic lymphadenitis

rows.label: Mimics
items: Reactive nodes: bilateral, mobile, recent URI; usually regress with observation
Atypical mycobacteria: chronic unilateral node, violaceous skin; excision rather than routine abscess incision
Lymphoma: rubbery, persistent nodes with systemic symptoms

table.title: Location → diagnosis → treatment
rows: SCM lump; ipsilateral tilt, opposite chin

pediatric-neck-masses.evidence: Checked 2026-11-05: [CHOP neck masses](https://www.chop.edu/conditions-diseases/neck-masses); established pediatric diagnostic approach.

pertussis.name: Pertussis
pertussis.scope: Bordetella pertussis, catarrhal, paroxysmal, and convalescent stages, posttussive emesis, inspiratory whoop, macrolide therapy, postexposure prophylaxis, Tdap vaccination
pertussis.core: Prolonged paroxysmal cough with posttussive emesis; infants may present with apnea and cyanosis without a whoop.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Unvaccinated/undervaccinated children, waning immunity in adolescents/adults, infected household contacts
Young infants have greatest risk of severe disease; vaccinated individuals can still transmit infection

rows.label: Clues
items: Catarrhal stage: rhinorrhea, mild cough, little or no fever; greatest early infectiousness
Inspiratory whoop often absent in adolescents/adults; convalescence can last weeks with recurrent cough
★ Infant **marked lymphocytosis**, poor feeding, or respiratory compromise; minimal fever despite serious illness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: B. pertussis adheres to respiratory cilia; toxin-mediated injury impairs mucus clearance
Pertussis toxin inhibits Gi signaling; impaired lymphocyte extravasation causes circulating lymphocytosis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Nasopharyngeal PCR** during first 3–4 weeks of cough; posterior nasopharynx, not throat swab
Culture most useful in first 2 weeks; late illness → validated serology when available
Treat suspected high-risk cases before results; chest imaging for respiratory compromise or suspected pneumonia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Azithromycin** preferred; TMP-SMX alternative at age ≥2 months when macrolides unsuitable
Best symptom benefit early; later treatment mainly reduces transmission within infectious window
Treat age ≥1 year within 3 weeks of cough; infants/pregnancy up to 6 weeks
Hospitalize young infants or apnea/hypoxemia; oxygen, suction, hydration and cardiorespiratory monitoring
Infant macrolides carry pyloric stenosis risk, but benefit outweighs risk; monitor vomiting

rows.label: Complications
items: Pneumonia, seizures/encephalopathy, infant pulmonary hypertension and death
Adults: rib fractures, syncope, stress incontinence from forceful coughing

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Droplet isolation until **5 days of effective antibiotics**, or 21 days from cough onset untreated
Household contacts → azithromycin prophylaxis within 21 days of index cough; also target high-risk exposures
DTaP childhood series; Tdap adolescent booster and once for adults without prior Tdap
★ **Tdap each pregnancy at 27–36 weeks**, preferably early in that interval

rows.label: Mimics
items: Viral bronchitis: improving ordinary cough without characteristic paroxysms or epidemiologic link
Asthma: recurrent wheeze/trigger pattern, reversible airflow obstruction
Chlamydial infant pneumonia: afebrile staccato cough, eosinophilia, often prior conjunctivitis

primary-immunodeficiencies.name: Primary immunodeficiencies
primary-immunodeficiencies.scope: Selective IgA deficiency, common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), X-linked agammaglobulinemia, severe combined immunodeficiency, hyper-IgE syndrome, Wiskott-Aldrich, chronic granulomatous disease
primary-immunodeficiencies.core: Recurrent, unusually severe, persistent, or opportunistic infections; organism pattern and age of onset localize the immune defect.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Consanguinity, affected relatives, male relatives dying in infancy; absent family history does not exclude disease

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, persistent thrush, or infections across multiple organ systems
Deep abscesses suggest phagocyte dysfunction; recurrent encapsulated bacteria suggest impaired antibody function

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Selective IgA deficiency: impaired mucosal defense; respiratory infections, giardiasis, atopy, or no symptoms
Antibody disorders impair opsonization; T-cell defects permit viral, fungal, and protozoal opportunists
DiGeorge: 3rd/4th **pharyngeal pouch** failure → absent thymus, hypocalcemia, conotruncal defects, T-cell infections
ADA deficiency: autosomal recessive SCID; toxic deoxyadenosine destroys T and B cells

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Start **CBC with differential, quantitative immunoglobulins**, HIV testing; assess vaccine antibody responses
Lymphocyte subsets distinguish B-cell and T-cell deficiencies; abnormal results → genetic confirmation
IgA deficiency: isolated IgA <7 mg/dL after age 4 years; normal IgG and IgM
★ Newborn **TREC screen** detects impaired T-cell production before symptomatic SCID

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Profound combined immune failure → isolation, irradiated CMV-negative blood products, urgent **transplant evaluation**
Acute infections: organism-directed antimicrobials; immunoglobulin replacement not useful for isolated IgA deficiency

rows.label: Complications
items: Bronchiectasis, chronic enteropathy, autoimmune disease; CVID additionally increases lymphoma risk
Anti-IgA antibodies can cause anaphylaxis to blood products

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Avoid **live vaccines** in major T-cell defects; immunize household contacts with safe vaccine choices
IgA-related transfusion reactions → washed cellular products or IgA-deficient plasma
CGD: TMP-SMX + itraconazole prophylaxis; genetic counseling for inherited defects

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vertical HIV: bacterial infections + zoster, nodes, maternal opportunistic infection; low CD4, positive virologic testing
Secondary hypogammaglobulinemia: nephrotic protein loss, B-cell malignancy, or rituximab exposure

table.title: Defect fingerprints
rows: Adolescent/adult; low IgG, poor vaccine response
Boy after 6 months; absent tonsils/B cells
Infant; absent thymic shadow, profound lymphopenia
Cold abscesses, eczema, retained teeth, pneumatoceles

proteinuria.name: Proteinuria
proteinuria.scope: Transient proteinuria, orthostatic (postural) proteinuria, persistent proteinuria, split urine collection, spot protein-to-creatinine ratio, nephrology referral
proteinuria.core: Incidental urinary protein requires confirmation and quantification; persistence, sediment, renal function, and blood pressure distinguish benign variants from kidney disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Transient: fever, strenuous exercise, dehydration, seizures; orthostatic pattern common in adolescent males
Persistent: diabetes, hypertension, glomerulonephritis, systemic autoimmune disease, hereditary nephropathy

rows.label: Clues
items: Often asymptomatic; foamy urine and periorbital/dependent edema suggest heavier losses
★ **Hematuria, hypertension, RBC casts, reduced eGFR**, or systemic rash/arthritis → pathologic renal process

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Glomerular permeability → albumin leakage; impaired tubular reabsorption → smaller proteins; overproduction → overflow

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Positive dipstick → **first-morning UA/microscopy and spot urine protein:creatinine ratio (UPCR)**
Pediatric normal UPCR: age >2 years **≤0.2 mg/mg**; age 6–24 months ≤0.5
Nephrotic range: children UPCR ≥2 mg/mg; adults total protein ≥3.5 g/day
★ Postural uncertainty → **split upright/supine collection**; separate daytime activity from overnight recumbency
Persistent abnormality → creatinine, albumin, BP; nephritic → complement/ANA; adults: spot albumin:creatinine

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Protein plus active sediment, impaired filtration, marked edema, or systemic disease → **nephrology referral**
Biopsy selected persistent unexplained cases, especially nephritic findings; do not biopsy benign postural pattern
Proteinuric CKD → ACE inhibitor/ARB when tolerated; treat diabetes/BP and underlying disease; monitor K/creatinine
Avoid empiric steroids before defining the syndrome; isolated low-grade protein does not establish nephrotic syndrome

rows.label: Complications
items: Sustained glomerular injury → CKD; heavy losses → hypoalbuminemia, thrombosis, infection
Benign transient/postural forms do not predict progressive renal failure

rows.label: Prevention
items: Control diabetes and hypertension, avoid nephrotoxins; assess family history and recurrent urinary abnormalities

rows.label: Mimics
items: False-positive dipstick: concentrated/alkaline urine, blood contamination; repeat clean specimen
Myeloma light chains: dipstick may be negative despite high total urine protein

shock.name: Shock
shock.scope: Hypovolemic, cardiogenic, distributive (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic), obstructive, fluid resuscitation, vasopressors
shock.core: Circulatory failure causing tissue hypoperfusion; normal blood pressure does not exclude early shock.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hemorrhage, GI losses, MI, infection, allergen exposure, spinal injury, thromboembolism
Recent surgery, immunosuppression, indwelling devices increase occult infection risk
Procedure bleeding: thoracentesis → intercostal artery, hemothorax; splenectomy → hemoperitoneum, left shoulder pain

rows.label: Clues
items: Tachycardia, altered mentation, oliguria, cool mottled skin; distributive forms may initially feel warm
★ **Anaphylaxis**: rapid airway swelling, wheezing, hypotension; skin findings may be absent
Neurogenic: **lost sympathetic tone** → hypotension, bradycardia or no tachycardia, warm skin after spinal cord injury

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Oxygen delivery falls below demand → anaerobic metabolism, lactate accumulation
Distributive vasodilation → relative hypovolemia despite normal total body fluid
Warm sepsis: high output, **high mixed venous O2**; pump failure: low contractility, congestion; hypovolemia: low preload

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Bedside ultrasound**: cardiac function, pericardial fluid, RV dilation, lung sliding, volume assessment
**Serial lactate**: hypoperfusion, best predicts course and mortality; trend with capillary refill, urine output
Septic shock: vasopressors for MAP ≥65 plus lactate >2 despite volume resuscitation
CBC, chemistry, ECG, troponin; cultures if infection suspected

rows.label: Tx
items: Airway, IV access; **isotonic crystalloid** (balanced, 0.9% saline) before imaging; restrict with pulmonary congestion
★ Hemorrhage → **control bleeding + blood products** (emergency O-negative); crystalloid as bridge; no vasopressors
★ Septic shock → antibiotics within 1 hour, drainage/debridement; crystalloid 30 mL/kg within 3 hours
★ Persistent septic hypotension → **norepinephrine**, MAP ≥65; add vasopressin, then epinephrine; refractory → hydrocortisone
Pulmonary edema after fluids → stop boluses, **inotrope**; children: epinephrine preferred, older exams may expect dopamine

rows.label: Complications
items: AKI, ischemic hepatitis, DIC, ARDS, bowel ischemia, multiorgan failure
Excess fluids → edema; vasopressors → digital/mesenteric ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early infection treatment, catheter hygiene, VTE prophylaxis, hemorrhage control
After anaphylaxis: trigger avoidance, epinephrine autoinjector, allergy referral

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vasovagal syncope: transient bradycardia, rapid recovery supine
Hypoglycemia: low bedside glucose, improvement with dextrose
Isolated head injury: hypertension + bradycardia (Cushing); trauma hypotension + tachycardia → assume hemorrhage

table.title: Hemodynamics and cause-directed rescue
rows: Decompress pneumothorax; drain tamponade; reperfuse PE

syphilis.name: Syphilis
syphilis.scope: Primary syphilis, secondary syphilis, latent syphilis, tertiary syphilis, neurosyphilis, serologic testing, Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, penicillin therapy
syphilis.core: Treponema pallidum infection progresses through mucocutaneous, asymptomatic, and destructive stages; neurologic, ocular, or auditory disease can occur anytime.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Unprotected sex, multiple partners, HIV; transplacental transmission during pregnancy

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Primary: **painless chancre** with regional lymphadenopathy
Secondary: palms/soles rash, condylomata lata, generalized nodes, patchy alopecia
Tertiary: gummas, ascending aortic aneurysm; tabes dorsalis, **Argyll Robertson pupils**, Charcot joint, or dementia
Latent: reactive serology without symptoms; early = acquired within 1 year

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Spirochete dissemination → endarteritis, young-adult meningovascular stroke; posterior column injury → sensory ataxia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **RPR/VDRL + treponemal assay**; discordant reverse screen → second treponemal assay
Early chancre with negative serology → lesion testing or repeat serology
★ Neurologic deficits → **LP**; CSF-VDRL specific, negative result does not exclude
Quantitative RPR: early disease follow-up at 6/12 months; latent at 6/12/24 months
Tertiary disease → CSF assessment before treatment; isolated ocular/otic disease may not require LP

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Pregnancy with penicillin allergy → **desensitization**, then stage-specific penicillin
Nonpregnant penicillin allergy, uncomplicated early infection → doxycycline for 14 days

rows.label: Complications
items: Jarisch-Herxheimer: fever/myalgias within 24 hours after treatment; supportive care, not allergy
Congenital infection → stillbirth, hearing loss, dental/bone abnormalities

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Partners exposed within **90 days** → presumptive early-syphilis treatment despite negative tests
Condoms; HIV testing; prenatal screening; serial RPR after treatment, fourfold rise suggests reinfection/failure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Chancroid: painful ulcer, tender suppurative nodes
HSV: painful grouped vesicles; pityriasis rosea: herald patch, usually spares palms
Autoimmune false-positive RPR: negative confirmatory treponemal assay

syphilis.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [CDC STI guidance](https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/syphilis.htm), including linked stage-specific guidance.

systemic-lupus-erythematosus.name: Systemic lupus erythematosus
systemic-lupus-erythematosus.scope: Diagnostic criteria (serositis, arthritis, lupus nephritis), neonatal lupus (congenital AV block), autoantibodies (ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith), pharmacotherapy (hydroxychloroquine, glucocorticoids)
systemic-lupus-erythematosus.core: Multisystem autoimmunity combining inflammatory joint, skin, serosal, renal, hematologic, or neurologic disease; flares often lower complement.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Reproductive-age women; family history; UV exposure, infections, estrogen-related triggers

rows.label: Clues
items: Photosensitive malar rash sparing nasolabial folds; painless oral ulcers; nonscarring alopecia
Symmetric nonerosive arthritis, pleuritic pain, pericarditis; leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hemolysis
★ **Proteinuria, RBC casts**, edema or hypertension → renal involvement
Neonatal lupus: maternal anti-Ro/SSA or anti-La/SSB; congenital AV block may be permanent

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immune-complex deposition activates **classical complement**, consuming C3/C4; autoantibody-mediated blood-cell destruction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ANA** sensitive entry test; anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm more specific
Anti-dsDNA titers, C3/C4, CBC, urinalysis, urine protein/creatinine, creatinine assess activity
★ Proteinuria **>0.5 g/g** or unexplained renal dysfunction → kidney biopsy
Classification: ANA ≥1:80, weighted score ≥10 with clinical criterion; clinical diagnosis remains contextual

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Hydroxychloroquine** broadly; NSAIDs for mild arthritis/serositis, glucocorticoids for flares
Organ-threatening flare → IV methylprednisolone; nephritis → mycophenolate plus belimumab/calcineurin inhibitor
Cyclophosphamide alternative for severe renal/CNS disease; taper glucocorticoids after disease control
Pregnancy → continue hydroxychloroquine; avoid mycophenolate, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide

rows.label: Complications
items: Accelerated atherosclerosis, infection, CKD; antiphospholipid antibodies → thrombosis or pregnancy loss
Hydroxychloroquine retinal toxicity; chronic steroid osteoporosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Sun protection; vaccines, cardiovascular risk control, retinal monitoring
Plan pregnancy during quiescence; anti-Ro/La positivity → fetal cardiac surveillance discussion

rows.label: Mimics
items: Drug-induced lupus: antihistone antibodies, usually no renal/CNS disease
Rheumatoid arthritis: erosions; fibromyalgia: pain without inflammatory findings

tick-borne-diseases.name: Tick-borne diseases
tick-borne-diseases.scope: Lyme disease, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, babesiosis, anaplasmosis, ehrlichiosis, doxycycline therapy
tick-borne-diseases.core: Outdoor exposure followed by multisystem illness: use rash pattern, blood counts, smear and cardiac/neurologic findings to distinguish vector-borne pathogens.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Northeast/upper Midwest Ixodes: Lyme, Babesia, Anaplasma; coinfection possible
Southeast/south-central US: RMSF, ehrlichiosis; absent bite recall cannot exclude
Asplenia, older age, immunosuppression → severe babesiosis

rows.label: Clues
items: Fever, headache, myalgias; hypotension, confusion or organ failure → hospitalize
Persistent fever on doxycycline or disproportionate anemia → consider coinfection

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Rickettsiae infect endothelium; Ehrlichia/Anaplasma infect leukocytes; Babesia infects RBCs
Borrelia spirochetes disseminate to skin, nervous system, heart, joints

rows.label: Dx
items: Early negative Lyme antibodies cannot exclude disease; isolated IgM after 30 days often misleading
★ **CBC, liver tests, creatinine**; anemia → hemolysis labs/smear; quantify babesial parasitemia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected **RMSF/ehrlichiosis/anaplasmosis → doxycycline immediately**, including children; never await results
Erythema migrans → doxycycline 10 days or amoxicillin 14 days; arthritis → oral treatment 28 days
Lyme high-grade block/PR ≥300 ms → admit, IV ceftriaxone ± pacing; meningitis → doxycycline/ceftriaxone
★ **Babesia: atovaquone + azithromycin**; consider exchange for parasitemia >10%, severe hemolysis or organ failure

rows.label: Complications
items: RMSF: DIC/renal failure; Lyme: facial palsy; Babesia: ARDS, relapse in immunosuppressed patients

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **DEET/picaridin, permethrin clothing, tick checks**, prompt removal with tweezers
High-risk Lyme bite: endemic Ixodes, attached ≥36 hours → single doxycycline dose within 72 hours
No prophylaxis for rickettsial disease; no Lyme testing after asymptomatic bite

rows.label: Mimics
items: Viral syndrome: worsening illness/cytopenias still warrant tick evaluation
TTP: schistocytes rather than intraerythrocytic parasites
Septic arthritis: toxic monoarthritis → aspirate rather than presume Lyme

vaginitis.name: Vaginitis
vaginitis.scope: Bacterial vaginosis, Trichomoniasis, Vulvovaginal candidiasis, atrophic vaginitis, genitourinary syndrome of menopause
vaginitis.core: Vaginal discharge or irritation requires distinction among dysbiosis, sexually transmitted protozoal infection, yeast overgrowth, and hypoestrogenic mucosal change.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: BV: new partners, douching; trichomoniasis: sexual exposure
Candida: antibiotics, pregnancy, diabetes, immunosuppression; atrophy: menopause or other hypoestrogenic states
Prepubertal: hand inoculation of respiratory pathogens during URI

rows.label: Clues
items: Pruritus, dysuria, dyspareunia; discharge appearance overlaps, so symptoms alone insufficient
★ **Fever, lower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness** → evaluate PID rather than isolated vaginitis
Postmenopausal bleeding needs assessment beyond assuming atrophy
★ Prepubertal **foul purulent/bloody discharge** → retained vaginal **foreign body**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: BV: lactobacilli depleted, anaerobes expand; Candida causes inflammatory overgrowth
Low estrogen thins epithelium and reduces lactobacilli → mucosal fragility and elevated vaginal pH

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Vaginal pH, saline/KOH microscopy**, history and examination; NAAT improves infectious diagnosis
BV: ≥3 Amsel—discharge, ↑pH, clue cells, amine odor; Gardnerella culture unhelpful (normal flora)
★ Suspected trichomoniasis + negative wet mount → **NAAT**, not reassurance
Recurrent/complicated Candida → culture or PCR for species; asymptomatic colonization alone needs no treatment

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Trichomoniasis → **oral metronidazole 7 days in women**; treat partners, abstain until completed/resolved
BV → oral metronidazole 7 days or vaginal metronidazole/clindamycin, **no routine partner treatment**, ACOG: treat if recurrent; treat symptomatic pregnancy
Candida → topical azole/nystatin or oral fluconazole; **pregnancy: topical azole 7 days**, avoid oral fluconazole
GSM → moisturizers/lubricants, then low-dose vaginal estrogen for persistent symptoms
Recurrent BV: ACOG 2025 considers male-partner metronidazole + topical clindamycin; older boards omit

rows.label: Complications
items: BV/trichomoniasis associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes and increased STI acquisition
Recurrent symptoms → reassess diagnosis, adherence, reinfection, diabetes or resistant/non-albicans yeast

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Trichomoniasis → **retest women at about 3 months**; condoms
Avoid douching/irritants; no routine partner treatment for uncomplicated Candida

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cervicitis: endocervical mucopus, friability, positive GC/CT NAAT
Contact dermatitis: external irritation after product exposure
Sarcoma botryoides: girl with bleeding, grape-like polypoid vaginal mass

valvular-heart-disease.name: Valvular heart disease
valvular-heart-disease.scope: Aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse, physical exam, echocardiography, surgical and transcatheter replacement
valvular-heart-disease.core: Murmur timing, location, radiation, and loading maneuvers localize valve disease; symptoms and ventricular response determine intervention.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Trileaflet calcification, age >70 → AS; rheumatic disease → MS
Bicuspid valve: murmur from youth, premature calcific AS (40s–60s); childhood **endocarditis**; adult aortic dissection
AR: endocarditis, dissection, **root dilation** (Marfan, hypertension; murmur along right sternal border)
MR: ischemia, myxomatous prolapse (connective tissue laxity), chamber dilation

rows.label: Clues
items: Exertional dyspnea, pulmonary edema, reduced exercise tolerance; abrupt deterioration suggests acute regurgitation
★ **Exertional syncope, angina, or HF** with obstruction → severe symptomatic disease
Squatting/handgrip increase regurgitant murmurs; standing/Valsalva → earlier MVP click, squatting → later

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Stenosis produces upstream pressure overload; regurgitation produces chamber volume overload
Acute regurgitation lacks compensatory dilation, rapidly elevating filling pressures and reducing forward output
Mitral stenosis: ↑LA pressure, ↑PCWP, ↑pulmonary artery pressure; **LVEDP normal**; AF abolishes presystolic accentuation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TTE Doppler** defines anatomy, severity, EF, chamber dimensions, pulmonary pressures
Severe AS: velocity ≥4 m/s, mean gradient ≥40, or valve area ≤1 cm²; discordance requires reassessment
Severe MS: valve area ≤1.5 cm²; TEE for thrombus before balloon intervention or uncertain anatomy
★ Acute murmur with shock → **urgent echocardiography**; TEE if endocarditis/dissection suspected

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute severe AR/MR → **urgent surgery**, stabilize with afterload reduction/diuresis if BP permits
Severe primary MR: **EF ≤60% or LVESD ≥40 mm** triggers intervention even without symptoms
Secondary MR → optimize HF treatment first; selected persistent severe cases benefit from transcatheter edge-to-edge repair
Avoid excessive preload reduction in severe AS; symptomatic relief never replaces needed valve intervention

rows.label: Complications
items: Heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, AF, systemic embolism, endocarditis
Mechanical prosthesis: thrombosis/bleeding; bioprosthesis: structural degeneration
Prosthetic dysfunction/paravalvular leak → new murmur, **schistocytes**, hemolytic anemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Warfarin for mechanical valves**; no DOAC substitution; rheumatic MS with AF also requires warfarin
Prosthetic valve or prior endocarditis → selected dental prophylaxis; native isolated MVP does not qualify
Periodic echo and symptom review; treat rheumatic fever to prevent recurrent valve injury

rows.label: Mimics
items: HCM: systolic murmur increases with Valsalva/standing
Aortic sclerosis: ejection murmur without significant gradient; flow murmur: normal valve anatomy

table.title: Valve signatures and definitive options
rows: Crescendo-decrescendo, carotids; soft A2; pulsus parvus et tardus
Early diastolic decrescendo; wide pulse pressure
Loud S1, opening snap, apical mid-diastolic rumble
Suitable symptomatic rheumatic valve → balloon commissurotomy
LLSB holosystolic, louder on inspiration; right HF

vitamin-k-deficiency.name: Vitamin K deficiency
vitamin-k-deficiency.scope: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding of newborn (VKDB), dietary deficiency, malabsorption, antibiotic-induced, coagulation factors (II, VII, IX, X), PT and PTT prolongation, intracranial hemorrhage
vitamin-k-deficiency.core: Unexplained bleeding with prolonged PT, especially after missed newborn prophylaxis or impaired fat absorption, suggests inadequate vitamin K-dependent coagulation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Newborn low stores, limited placental transfer, low breast-milk content; prophylaxis refusal
Cholestasis, pancreatic insufficiency, intestinal malabsorption; poor intake plus prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics
Warfarin inhibits recycling; maternal enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs increase early neonatal risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Umbilical, GI, skin/mucosal or procedural bleeding; infant may initially appear well
★ Late infant bleeding may present as **intracranial hemorrhage**, seizures, pallor or bulging fontanelle
Adult deficiency usually requires poor nutrition plus malabsorption, altered flora or medication effects

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ★ Impaired γ-carboxylation of **II (prothrombin), VII, IX, X, proteins C/S** → deficient thrombin activation
Factor VII shortest half-life → PT prolongs first; severe deficiency also prolongs aPTT

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **PT/INR**, aPTT, CBC/platelets, fibrinogen; platelets and fibrinogen usually normal
Mixing study corrects factor deficiency; factor V preserved unlike substantial hepatic synthetic failure
Rapid coagulation improvement after phytonadione supports diagnosis; investigate underlying cholestasis/malabsorption

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Phytonadione** replacement; parenteral route for serious bleeding or unreliable absorption
Life-threatening bleeding → IV vitamin K plus **4-factor PCC or FFP** for immediate factor replacement
Stabilize airway/circulation, transfuse RBCs if needed; suspected infant intracranial bleeding → urgent head imaging
Correct malabsorption, poor intake and culprit antibiotics; never delay emergency hemostasis for confirmation

rows.label: Complications
items: Intracranial hemorrhage → death or lasting neurologic disability; hemorrhagic shock
Rare anaphylactoid reactions with IV phytonadione; use monitored slow infusion

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Newborns >1500 g: **vitamin K 1 mg IM within 6 hours**; smaller infants: weight-based dosing
Oral newborn prophylaxis less reliable against late VKDB; IM prophylaxis preferred
Identify cholestatic infants and provide ongoing replacement when absorption impaired

rows.label: Mimics
items: DIC: low platelets/fibrinogen with elevated D-dimer
Hemophilia: isolated prolonged aPTT, normal PT
Liver failure: other synthetic dysfunction, often low factor V

table.title: VKDB timing
rows: Maternal drugs interfering with vitamin K
No prophylaxis, exclusive breastfeeding, occult cholestasis
